questions.stem: What is the news report mainly about?
options: A) The return of a bottled message to its owner's daughter.
B) A New Hampshire man's joke with friends on his wife.
C) A father's message for his daughter.
D) The history of a century-old motel.

explain.定位:
A message in a bottle sent out to sea by a New Hampshire man more than five decades ago
was found 1,500 miles away and has been returned to his daughter.
一封五十多年前被一位新罕布什尔州男子投入大海的瓶中信，在一千五百英里之外被发现，
如今已归还给他的女儿。
explain.信号:
新闻首句即中心句。这句是录音的开头第一句 A message in a bottle sent out to sea by
a New Hampshire man more than five decades ago was found 1,500 miles away and
has been returned to his daughter.，新闻播报惯于把最核心的事件放在导语首句，它把
瓶中信、被发现、归还给女儿三件事一次说全，正是全篇主线。
explain.替换:
has been returned to his daughter ↔ The return of a bottled message to its owner's daughter
动词转名词的同义改写
A message in a bottle ↔ a bottled message
短语等价改写
explain.排除:
B) 原词陷阱
原文确实提到这位男子写字条是 as a joke（开个玩笑），B 盗用了 joke 这个原词诱你选；
但原文从没说这玩笑是开给 friends 朋友、更没说开在 his wife 妻子身上，B 把玩笑的对象
凭空换成了朋友和妻子，且玩笑只是背景细节、撑不起全篇主旨。
借用原文：Her father had written the notes as a joke
C) 答非所问
原文是讲过一位父亲为女儿留下字条这件事，C 借此设套；但 A father's message for his
daughter. 只截取了故事的起因，丢掉了这封信漂流五十年又被陌生人寻回归还的核心情
节，作为主旨太窄，覆盖不了首句强调的 return 归还这条主线。
借用原文：The motel was owned by the parents of Paula Pierce
D) 原词陷阱
原文出现了 Beachcomber Motel、The motel was owned by the parents of Paula
Pierce，D 盗用 motel 这个原词；但旅馆只是字条里留的归还地址这一背景，原文根本没讲
它的 history 历史、也没说它 century-old 有百年，D 是顺着熟词造出的跑题项。
借用原文：owners of the Beachcomber Motel

questions.stem: Why did Paula Pierce give Clint Buffington the reward?
options: A) She wanted to show gratitude for his kindness.
B) She wanted to honor her father's promise.
C) She had been asked by her father to do so.
D) She was excited to see her father's handwriting.

explain.定位:
She held up to her father's promise, giving Buffington that reward.
她信守了父亲的承诺，把那笔酬金给了巴芬顿。
explain.信号:
给酬金动作旁的动机句。答案就在描述给酬金这个动作的同一句里 She held up to her
father's promise, giving Buffington that reward.——前半句 held up to her father's
promise 正是她给酬金的原因，后半句 giving Buffington that reward 才是行为本身，原
因与行为同句出现，是最直接的动机信号。
explain.替换:
She held up to her father's promise ↔ She wanted to honor her father's promise
动词近义替换
explain.排除:
A) 未提及
原文末句确有 the biggest reward is the message in a bottle finding its way back
home 谈到这件事温暖的一面，A 借这种暖意诱你联想到感激；但原文从没说她给酬金是为
了 show gratitude 表达感激、也没提对方的 kindness 好意，给酬金的真正原因是守父亲
承诺，A 属凭印象添的动机。
C) 偷换概念
原文反复出现 father 和 promise，C 盗用 her father 这个原词，且 She had been asked
by her father to do so. 与正确项只差一层意思，极易混；但原文说的是字条是父亲多年前
写下的承诺、由她主动信守，并没有父亲当面 asked her 要求她这么做这一情节，C 把主动
守诺偷换成被父亲吩咐。
借用原文：She held up to her father's promise
D) 答非所问
原文确实提到字条上是父亲 had written the notes 亲笔写的，D 盗用 father、
handwriting 相关的线索；但 She was excited to see her father's handwriting. 说的是
看到父亲笔迹很激动，这是一种情绪反应，答的根本不是 Why 给酬金这个问题，与题干所
问错位。
借用原文：Her father had written the notes
Questions 3 and 4 are based on the news report you have just heard.
1 Millions of bees have died in South Carolina during aerial insect spraying operations that were carried
out to combat the Zika virus. The insects spraying over the weekend left more than 2 million bees dead
on the spot in Dorchester County, South Carolina, where four travel-related cases of Zika disease have
been confirmed in the area. Most of the deaths came from Flower Town Bee farm, a company in
Somerville that sells bees and honey products. Juanita Stanley who owns the company said the farm
"looks like it's been destroyed." The farm lost about 2.5 million bees. Dorchester County officials
apologized for the accidental mass killing of bees. Dorchester County is aware that some beekeepers in
the area that was sprayed on Sunday lost their bee colonies. County manager Jason Ward said in a
statement. "I'm not pleased that so many bees were killed."
数百万只蜜蜂在South Carolina为对抗Zika病毒而进行的空中喷洒杀虫剂行动中死亡。周末的喷洒行动导
致South Carolina的Dorchester County超过200万只蜜蜂当场死亡，该地区已确诊四例与旅行相关的
Zika病例。大部分死亡来自Flower Town Bee farm,这是Somerville一家销售蜜蜂和蜂蜜产品的公司。公
司所有者Juanita Stanley说，农场"看起来像是被摧毁了"。该农场损失了约250万只蜜蜂。Dorchester
County官员为意外大规模杀死蜜蜂一事道歉。Dorchester County意识到周日喷洒区域内的一些养蜂人
失去了他们的蜂群。县管理人员Jason Ward在一份声明中说："我对如此多的蜜蜂被杀死感到不满。"

questions.stem: Why were spraying operations carried out in Dorchester County?
options: A) People were concerned about the number of bees.
B) Several cases of Zika disease had been identified.
C) Two million bees were infected with disease.
D) Zika virus had destroyed some bee farms.

explain.定位:
Millions of bees have died in South Carolina during aerial insect spraying operations that
were carried out to combat the Zika virus.
在南卡罗来纳州为对抗 Zika 病毒而开展的空中杀虫喷药行动中，数百万只蜜蜂死亡。
explain.信号:
carried out to 直接交代目的起因。答案句里 carried out to combat the Zika virus
用‘carried out to + 动词’点明喷药的目的就是‘对抗 Zika 病毒’，这正是题干 Why 要的起
因。‘to + 动词’的目的结构就是原因题的答案信号。
explain.替换:
carried out to combat the Zika virus ↔ Several cases of Zika disease had been identified
为对抗病毒 ↔ 已确认有病例
four travel-related cases of Zika disease have been confirmed ↔
Several cases of Zika disease had been identified
four…confirmed ↔ Several…identified
explain.排除:
A) 答非所问
录音确实反复提到 bees 大量死亡，A 的 concerned about the number of bees 借了‘蜜
蜂数量’这个听感很熟的点。但蜜蜂死亡是喷药的‘后果’，不是喷药的‘起因’；喷药的起因是对
抗病毒。A 答非所问，把后果当成了原因。
借用原文：left more than 2 million bees dead on the spot
C) 原词陷阱
录音念到 more than 2 million bees dead（两百多万只蜜蜂死亡），C 的 Two million
bees were infected with disease 直接搬来 ‘Two million’ 这个数字来骗‘听到了就想选’。
但蜜蜂是被喷药‘毒死’的，不是‘感染疾病’；得病的是人（有病例），不是蜜蜂。C 偷换了死
因，是典型原词陷阱。
借用原文：left more than 2 million bees dead on the spot
D) 张冠李戴
录音里 Zika、destroyed 这两个词都真出现过——农场主说农场 looks like it's been
destroyed，但毁掉蜂场的是‘喷的药’，不是‘Zika 病毒’。D 的 Zika virus had destroyed
some bee farms 把毁场的元凶张冠李戴给了病毒，强加了错误因果。
借用原文：looks like it's been destroyed

questions.stem: What does the news report say about Flowertown Bee Farm?
options: A) It apologized to its customers.
B) It was forced to kill its bees.
C) It lost a huge stock of bees.

explain.定位:
Most of the deaths came from Flower Town Bee farm, a company in Somerville that sells
bees and honey products. Juanita Stanley who owns the company said the farm "looks like it's
been destroyed." The farm lost about 2.5 million bees.
大部分死亡蜜蜂来自位于萨默维尔、售卖蜜蜂和蜂蜜制品的 Flower Town 蜂场。蜂场主胡
安妮塔·斯坦利说农场"看上去像是被毁了"。这家蜂场损失了约 250 万只蜜蜂。
explain.信号:
专有名词后紧跟的损失陈述。Flower Town Bee farm 这个名字出现后，紧跟的 The farm
lost about 2.5 million bees 直接交代了这家农场的遭遇，正是题干 ‘say about
Flowertown Bee Farm’ 要的内容。专有名词后第一句关于它的陈述就是答案句。
explain.替换:
The farm lost about 2.5 million bees ↔ It lost a huge stock of bees
lost 2.5 million bees ↔ lost a huge stock of bees
explain.排除:
A) 张冠李戴
录音里 apologized 确实念到了——但道歉的是 Dorchester County officials apologized
（多切斯特县官员道歉），不是这家农场，更没说向 ‘customers（顾客）’道歉。A 的 It
apologized to its customers 把道歉者从‘县政府’张冠李戴成了‘农场’，主体搞反。
借用原文：Dorchester County officials apologized for the accidental mass killing of bees
B) 原词陷阱
录音里 kill 出现在 accidental mass killing of bees（意外大规模杀死蜜蜂）和县经理那句
so many bees were killed，B 借了 ‘kill’ 这个词。但蜜蜂是被喷药‘误杀/意外致死’的，农场
是受害者，并非 ‘forced to kill its bees（被迫杀死自己的蜂）’。B 把‘被误杀’偷换成‘被迫主
动杀’。
借用原文：accidental mass killing of bees
D) 原词陷阱
录音念到 lost about 2.5 million bees，单位是‘只蜜蜂’；D 的 It lost 2.5 million dollars
直接搬来 ‘2.5 million’ 这个数字，却把单位偷偷换成 dollars（美元）。录音从没说损失了
多少钱，D 是靠数字相同来骗选的原词陷阱。
借用原文：The farm lost about 2.5 million bees

questions.stem: What do we learn about the first flight of the Airlander 10?
options: A) It stayed in the air for about two hours.
B) It took off and landed on a football field.
C) It proved to be of high commercial value.
D) It made a series of sharp turns in the sky.

explain.定位:
The Air lander 10 spent nearly two hours in the air, having taken off from Coddington
Airfield in Bedfordshire.
“飞行者 10 号”在空中停留了近两个小时，此前它从贝德福德郡的科丁顿机场起飞。
explain.信号:
紧跟开头点题句的首句事实，含时间数字。新闻在首句 The world's largest aircraft has
taken to the skies for the first time. 点题后，紧接着用 spent nearly two hours in the
air 给出首飞的核心事实，时间数字就是答案信号——新闻里报出的具体数字几乎必是
考点。
explain.替换:
spent nearly two hours in the air ↔ It stayed in the air for about two hours.
spent...in the air = stayed in the air；nearly two hours = about two hours
explain.排除:
B) 原词陷阱
选项 It took off and landed on a football field. 盗用了录音里的 as long as a football
field 和 taken off：但 football field 是用来形容它“和足球场一样长”的体型，不是起降地
点；真正的起飞地是 Coddington Airfield in Bedfordshire，且录音根本没说在球场降落，
属听到原词就误选。
借用原文：as long as a football field
C) 未提及
选项 It proved to be of high commercial value. 在录音里找不到对应：原文只说造价、载
重、噪音排放，从未评价它“已证明有高商业价值”；这是把首飞事实拔高成商业结论的合理
想象。
D) 与原文相反
选项 It made a series of sharp turns in the sky. 盗用了录音 performed a series of
gentle turns 里的 a series of...turns，但偷偷把 gentle（平缓）改成了 sharp（急），程
度正好相反；听到“一连串转弯”就选，会栽在这个程度词上。
借用原文：performed a series of gentle turns

questions.stem: What causes the US government to abandon the Airlander 10 as a spy aircraft?
options: B) The air pollution it produced.
D) The opposition from the military.

explain.定位:
It was first developed for the US government as a long-range spy aircraft, but was abandoned
following budget cutbacks.
它最初是为美国政府研发的一种远程侦察机，但因预算削减而被放弃。
explain.信号:
因果信号 following 紧跟在 abandoned 之后。答案信号是 abandoned following
budget cutbacks 里的 following——它等于“由于/在……之后”，紧跟其后的 budget
cutbacks 就是导致放弃的原因；following 在这里就是 because of 的同义因果词，听到它
要立刻抓后面的名词。
explain.替换:
budget cutbacks ↔ Inadequate funding
budget cutbacks（削减预算）≈ inadequate funding（资金不足）
explain.排除:
A) 未提及
选项 Engineering problems 在录音里没有任何依据：原文讲放弃的原因只有预算削减，从
没说出过技术/工程故障；这是凭“高科技飞行器易出技术问题”的常识脑补的原因。
B) 原词陷阱
选项 The air pollution it produced 盗用了录音里的 pollution 一词，但原文 emitting
less pollution 说的是它“排放更少污染”、是优点，根本不是被放弃的原因；听到 pollution
就选，正好掉进原词陷阱并且把优点错当原因。
借用原文：emitting less pollution
D) 未提及
选项 The opposition from the military 借“为美国政府研发的侦察机”勾起军事联想，但录
音只字未提军方反对；developed for the US government 只说明用途，没说军方反对
它，属听到军事背景就顺势脑补。

questions.stem: What is the advantage of the Airlander 10 over huge jet planes?
options: A) It uses the latest aviation technology.
B) It flies faster than a commercial jet.
C) It is a safer means of transportation.
D) It is more environmentally friendly.

explain.定位:
The aircraft cost 25 million pounds and can carry heavier loads than huge jet planes while
also producing less noise and emitting less pollution.
这架飞行器造价 2500 万英镑，能比大型喷气式飞机运载更重的货物，同时产生的噪音更
小、排放的污染也更少。
explain.信号:
than huge jet planes 的对比句，重点落在 less noise/less pollution。答案信号是
than huge jet planes 这个明确对比——它把本物和题干里的 huge jet planes 摆在一起
比，紧接着的 producing less noise and emitting less pollution 给出环保维度的优势，
正是答案落点。
explain.替换:
producing less noise and emitting less pollution ↔ It is more environmentally friendly.
less noise + less pollution 概括为 more environmentally friendly
explain.排除:
A) 原词陷阱
选项 It uses the latest aviation technology. 借录音末尾的 the aviation administration
等航空字眼制造“高科技”印象，但原文从没说它用了“最新航空技术”；这是听到 aviation 就
联想“先进技术”的原词/话题陷阱。
借用原文：the aviation administration
B) 答非所问
选项 It flies faster than a commercial jet. 盗用了对比结构 than...jet，但录音里和 jet
planes 比的是 carry heavier loads（载重更重），从没说飞得更快；把对比维度从载重/环
保偷换成速度，是答非所问。
借用原文：can carry heavier loads than huge jet planes
C) 未提及
选项 It is a safer means of transportation. 在录音里没有依据：原文讲的优势是载重大、
噪音小、污染少，从没说它“更安全”；这是把“好处”顺手脑补成“安全”的合理想象。

questions.stem: What does the woman think of climate change?
options: A) It seems a depressing topic.
C) It has little impact on our daily life.
D) It is getting more serious these days.

explain.定位:
Well, it sounds really awful. It's an important subject, I agree, but I'm not in the mood for
anything depressing.
嗯，这听起来太糟糕了。我承认这是个重要的话题，但我没心情看任何令人沮丧的东西。
explain.信号:
转折 but 后才是真态度。前半 It's an important subject, I agree 是先让一步，真正的态
度在 but I'm not in the mood for anything depressing 这个转折之后——but 后面那句
才是女士对这话题的真实评价。
explain.替换:
anything depressing ↔ a depressing topic
原词 depressing 直接对应
it sounds really awful ↔ a depressing topic
awful 与 depressing 同向负评
explain.排除:
B)
It sounds quite alarming. 的 alarming（令人警觉）在录音里从未出现，女士说的是
awful、depressing，是另造了一个情绪词来混淆，与原文不符。
C)
It has little impact on our daily life. 说"对日常生活没什么影响"，但录音里女士承认 It's
an important subject（这是个重要话题），恰恰认为它重要，C 与原文意思相反。
D)
It is getting more serious these days. 说气候变化"越来越严重"，听感上与 It's an
important subject"重要"沾边，但 important（重要）不等于 getting more serious（越
来越严重），且女士全程没说"越来越严重"，是借"重要"的语感诱选。
借用原文：It's an important subject

questions.stem: Why do the speakers give up going to the Spanish Dance Festival tonight?
options: A) The man doesn't understand Spanish.
B) The woman doesn't really like dancing.
C) They don't want something too noisy.
D) They can't make it to the theatre in time.

explain.定位:
Well, that's no good. We haven't got enough time to get there. Is there anything else?
唉，那不行。我们没有足够的时间赶到那儿。还有别的吗？
explain.信号:
否定句 that's no good 引出原因。女士先在前一段问几点开演、男士答 At 7:30.，紧接着
女士说 that's no good（那不行），后面那句 We haven't got enough time to get there
就是放弃的真正原因——否定评价后紧跟的解释句即落点。
explain.替换:
We haven't got enough time to get there ↔ They can't make it to the theatre in time
时间不够 = 来不及赶到
explain.排除:
A) 原词陷阱
The man doesn't understand Spanish. 借了录音里 Spanish Dance Festival 的 Spanish
一词，但录音从没说男士"听不懂西班牙语"，这是听到 Spanish 就想选的典型原词陷阱。
借用原文：Spanish Dance Festival
B)
The woman doesn't really like dancing. 说女士不喜欢跳舞，可录音里她明明说 I love
dance（我喜欢跳舞），态度恰好相反，B 与原文反向。
借用原文：I love dance
C) 未提及
They don't want something too noisy. 说"不想要太吵的"，但录音里两人放弃舞蹈节的理
由是时间，从没提"吵"，这一项属无中生有。

questions.stem: What does the critic say about the comedy performed at the City Theatre?
options: A) It would be more fun without Mr. Whitehead hosting.
B) It has too many acts to hold the audience's attention.
C) It is the most amusing show he has ever watched.
D) It is a show inappropriate for a night of charity.

explain.定位:
The critic in the local paper says it's the funniest thing he's ever seen.
当地报纸的评论家说，这是他看过的最有趣的东西。
explain.信号:
最高级 the funniest…ever 是落点。The critic in the local paper says it's the funniest
thing he's ever seen 用了最高级 the funniest…he's ever seen（他看过最有趣的），最高
级常是答案信号，且明确标出说话人是 the critic，正好对上题干问的主语。
explain.替换:
it's the funniest thing he's ever seen ↔ It is the most amusing show he has ever watched
funniest = most amusing 最高级对最高级
explain.排除:
A)
It would be more fun without Mr. Whitehead hosting.（没 Whitehead 主持会更好玩）
盗用了录音里的人名 Mr. Whitehead，但嫌他不好笑的是女士 I'm not keen on him. He's
not very funny.，不是评论家；题干问的是 critic，这是张冠李戴。
借用原文：He's not very funny
B)
It has too many acts to hold the audience's attention. 借了录音 lots of different acts
（很多不同节目）里的 acts 一词，但原文是中性陈述"有很多节目"，绝没有说"节目太多抓
不住观众注意力"，是把"多"歪曲成"太多以致没法吸引人"。
借用原文：lots of different acts
D)
It is a show inappropriate for a night of charity. 说它"不适合慈善之夜"，但录音里它正
是 a charity comedy night，评论家还夸它最好笑，根本没说"不合适"，D 与原文相反、属
无中生有。
借用原文：charity comedy night

questions.stem: What is the researchers' purpose in carrying out the series of experiments with mice?
options: A) To investigate how being overweight impacts on health.
B) To find out which physical drive is the most powerful.
C) To discover what most mice like to eat.
D) To determine what feelings mice have.

explain.定位:
In the study, researchers found that hunger outweighed other physical drives, including fear,
thirst and social needs. To determine which feeling won out, the researchers did a series
of experiments.
在这项研究中，研究者发现饥饿胜过了其他生理驱动力，包括恐惧、口渴和社交需求。为了
确定哪种感觉占上风，研究者做了一系列实验。

which feeling won out, the researchers did a series of experiments.——'为确定哪种感
觉占上风而做实验'，正是研究者做这串实验的目的，目的状语句就是目的题的落点。
explain.替换:
which feeling won out ↔ which physical drive is the most powerful
won out=最强 同义改写
explain.排除:

overweight 的话题感，但录音通篇讲的是比较饥饿等驱动力，从未把研究目的定为'肥胖对
健康的影响'，是答非所问。

验是比较饥饿与恐惧、口渴、社交，并非研究老鼠'爱吃什么'，把宏大的目的偷换成了一个
没做的小问题。

the food

feeling won out 的 determine、feeling 原词，极具迷惑性；但录音是'确定哪种感觉占上
风（最强）'，不是'确定老鼠有哪些感觉'，把'比较强弱'偷换成了'清点种类'。

questions.stem: In what circumstances, do mice venture into unsafe areas?

explain.定位:
It turned out that, when the mice were hungry, they ventured into the unsafe areas

questions.stem: What does the speaker say about the American highway system?

是 just after World War I(一战刚结束后)军方才想建——时间正好相反，听到 "World

options: A) To improve transportation in the countryside.
B) To move troops quickly from place to place.
C) To enable people to travel at a higher speed.
D) To speed up the transportation of goods.

system for national defense. Such a system could, if necessary, move troops quickly from one
area to another.
在那些年，也就是一战刚结束后，军方想为国防而修建一套美国公路系统。这样一套系统在
必要时可以把军队从一个地区迅速调往另一个地区。

的的介词短语锁定——它是录音里讲到的 "最初" 动机，紧接着的 move troops quickly
from one area to another 是对这一目的的具体展开。

move troops quickly from one area to another ↔ To move troops quickly from place to place.

——题目问哪件事，就找那件事旁边的年份。

questions.stem: A student's yearly expenses on access codes may amount to their rent for two months.
questions.passage:
Some College Students Are Angry That They Have to Pay to Do Their Homework

A) Digital learning systems now charge students for access codes needed to complete coursework, take quizzes, and turn in homework. As universities go digital, students are complaining of a new hit to their finances that's replacing—and sometimes joining—expensive textbooks: pricey online access codes that are required to complete coursework and submit assignments.

B) The codes—which typically range in price from $80 to $155 per course—give students online access to systems developed by education companies like McGraw Hill and Pearson. These companies, which long reaped big profits as textbook publishers, have boasted that their new online offerings, when pushed to students through universities they partner with, represent the future of the industry.

C) But critics say the digital access codes represent the same profit-seeking ethos(观念) of the textbook business, and are even harder for students to opt out of. While they could once buy second-hand textbooks, or share copies with friends, the digital systems are essentially impossible to avoid.

D) "When we talk about the access code we see it as the new face of the textbook monopoly(垄断), a new way to lock students around this system," said Ethan Senack, the higher education advocate for the U.S. Public Interest Research Group, to BuzzFeed News. "Rather than $250 (for a print textbook) you're paying $120," said Senack. "But because it's all digital it eliminates the used book market and eliminates any sharing and because homework and tests are through an access code, it eliminates any ability to opt out."

E) Sarina Harper, a 19-year-old student at Virginia Tech, was faced with a tough dilemma when she first started college in 2015—pay rent or pay to turn in her chemistry homework. She told BuzzFeed News that her freshman chemistry class required her to use Connect, a system provided by McGraw Hill where students can submit homework, take exams and track their grades. But the code to access the program cost $120—a big sum for Harper, who had already put down $450 for textbooks, and had rent day approaching.

F) She decided to wait for her next work-study paycheck, which was typically $150–$200, to pay for the code. She knew that her chemistry grade may take a dive as a result. "It's a balancing act," she said. "Can I really afford these access codes now?" She didn't hand in her first two assignments for chemistry, which started her out in the class with a failing grade.

G) The access codes may be another financial headache for students, but for textbook businesses, they're the future. McGraw Hill, which controls 21% of the higher education market, reported in March that its digital content sales exceeded print sales for the first time in 2015. The company said that 45% of its $140 million revenue in 2015 "was derived from digital products."

H) A Pearson spokesperson told BuzzFeed News that "digital materials are less expensive and a good investment" that offers new features, like audio texts, personalized knowledge checks and expert videos. Its digital course materials save students up to 60% compared to traditional printed textbooks, the company added. McGraw Hill didn't respond to a request for comment, but its CEO David Levin told the Financial Times in August that "in higher education, the era of the printed textbook is now over."

I) The textbook industry insists the online systems represent a better deal for students. "These digital products aren't just mechanisms for students to submit homework, they offer all kinds of features," David Anderson, the executive director of higher education with the Association of American Publishers, told BuzzFeed News. "It helps students understand in a way that you can't do with print homework assignments."

J) David Hunt, an associate professor in sociology at Augusta University, which has rolled out digital textbooks across its math and psychology departments, told BuzzFeed News that he understands the utility of using systems that require access codes. But he doesn't require his students to buy access to a learning program that controls the class assignments. "I try to make things as inexpensive as possible," said Hunt, who uses free digital textbooks for his classes but designs his own curriculum. "The online systems may make my life a lot easier but I feel like I'm giving up control. The discussions are the things where my expertise can benefit the students most."

K) A 20-year-old junior at Georgia Southern University told BuzzFeed News that she normally spends $500–$600 on access codes for class. In one case, the professor didn't require students to buy a textbook, just an access code to turn in homework. This year she said she spent $900 on access codes to books and programs. "That's two months of rent," she said. "You can't sell any of it back. With a traditional textbook you can sell it for $30–$50 and that helps to pay for your new semester's books. With an access code, you're out of that money."

L) Benjamin Wolverton, a 19-year-old student at the University of South Carolina, told BuzzFeed News that "it's ridiculous that after paying tens of thousands in tuition we have to pay for all these access codes to do our homework." Many of the access codes he's purchased have been required simply to complete homework or quizzes. "Often it's only 10% of your grade in class." he said. "You're paying so much money for something that hardly affects your grade—but if you didn't have it, it would affect your grade enough. It would be bad to start out at a B or C." Wolverton said he spent $500 on access codes for digital books and programs this semester.

M) Harper, a poultry(家禽) science major, is taking chemistry again this year and had to buy a new access code to hand in her homework. She rented her economics and statistics textbooks for about $20 each. But her access codes for homework, which can't be rented or bought second-hand, were her most expensive purchases: $120 and $85.

N) She still remembers the sting of her first experience skipping an assignment due to the high prices. "We don't really have a missed assignment policy," she said. "If you miss it, you just miss it. I just got zeros on a couple of first assignments. I managed to pull everything back up. But as a scared freshman looking at their grades, it's not fun."

questions.passage:

A) Digital learning systems now charge students for access codes needed to complete coursework, take quizzes, and turn in homework. As universities go digital, students are complaining of a new hit to their finances that's replacing—and sometimes joining—expensive textbooks: pricey online access codes that are required to complete coursework and submit assignments.

B) The codes—which typically range in price from $80 to $155 per course—give students online access to systems developed by education companies like McGraw Hill and Pearson. These companies, which long reaped big profits as textbook publishers, have boasted that their new online offerings, when pushed to students through universities they partner with, represent the future of the industry.

C) But critics say the digital access codes represent the same profit-seeking ethos(观念) of the textbook business, and are even harder for students to opt out of. While they could once buy second-hand textbooks, or share copies with friends, the digital systems are essentially impossible to avoid.

D) "When we talk about the access code we see it as the new face of the textbook monopoly(垄断), a new way to lock students around this system," said Ethan Senack, the higher education advocate for the U.S. Public Interest Research Group, to BuzzFeed News. "Rather than $250 (for a print textbook) you're paying $120," said Senack. "But because it's all digital it eliminates the used book market and eliminates any sharing and because homework and tests are through an access code, it eliminates any ability to opt out."

E) Sarina Harper, a 19-year-old student at Virginia Tech, was faced with a tough dilemma when she first started college in 2015—pay rent or pay to turn in her chemistry homework. She told BuzzFeed News that her freshman chemistry class required her to use Connect, a system provided by McGraw Hill where students can submit homework, take exams and track their grades. But the code to access the program cost $120—a big sum for Harper, who had already put down $450 for textbooks, and had rent day approaching.

The company said that 45% of its $140 million revenue in 2015 "was derived from digital products."

"That's two months of rent," she said. "You can't sell any of it back. With a traditional textbook you can sell it for $30–$50 and that helps to pay for your new semester's books. With an access code, you're out of that money."

Wolverton said he spent $500 on access codes for digital books and programs this semester.

She rented her economics and statistics textbooks for about $20 each. But her access codes for homework, which can't be rented or bought second-hand, were her most expensive purchases: $120 and $85.

questions.stem: Why does the author say that one needn't be concerned about memory slips?
options: A) Not all of them are symptoms of dementia.
B) They occur only among certain groups of people.
C) Not all of them are related to one's age.
D) They are quite common among fifty-year-olds.
questions.passage:
Losing your ability to think and remember is pretty scary. We know the risk of dementia (痴呆症) increases with age. But if you have memory slips, you probably needn't worry. There are pretty clear differences between signs of dementia and age-related memory loss.

After age 50, it's quite common to have trouble remembering the names of people, places and things quickly, says Dr. Kirk Daffner of Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston.

The brain ages just like the rest of the body. Certain parts shrink, especially areas in the brain that are important to learning, memory and planning. Changes in brain cells can affect communication between different regions of the brain. And blood flow can be reduced as blood vessels narrow.

Forgetting the name of an actor in a favorite movie, for example, is nothing to worry about. But if you forget the plot of the movie or don't remember even seeing it, that's far more concerning, Daffner says.

When you forget entire experiences, he says, that's "a red flag that something more serious may be involved." Forgetting how to operate a familiar object like a microwave oven, or forgetting how to drive to the house of a friend you've visited many times before can also be signs of something going wrong.

But even then, Daffner says, people shouldn't panic. There are many things that can cause confusion and memory loss, including health problems like temporary stoppage of breathing during sleep, high blood pressure, or depression, as well as medications(药物)like antidepressants.

You don't have to figure this out on your own. Daffner suggests going to your doctor to check on medications, health problems and other issues that could be affecting memory. And the best defense against memory loss is to try to prevent it by building up your brain's cognitive(认知的)reserve, Daffner says.

"Read books, go to movies, take on new hobbies or activities that force one to think in novel ways," he says. In other words, keep your brain busy and working. And also get physically active, because exercise is a known brain booster.

Losing your ability to think and remember is pretty scary. We know the risk of dementia (痴呆症) increases with age. But if you have memory slips, you probably needn't worry. There are pretty clear differences between signs of dementia and age-related memory loss.

The brain ages just like the rest of the body. Certain parts shrink, especially areas in the brain that are important to learning, memory and planning. Changes in brain cells can affect communication between different regions of the brain. And blood flow can be reduced as blood vessels narrow.

questions.stem: What happened to Darwin's letter in the 1970s?
options: A) It was recovered by the FBI.
B) It was stolen more than once.
C) It was put in the archives for research purposes.
D) It was purchased by the Smithsonian Archives.
questions.passage:
A letter written by Charles Darwin in 1875 has been returned to the Smithsonian Institution Archives(档案馆) by the FBI after being stolen twice.

"We realized in the mid-1970s that it was missing," says Effie Kapsalis, head of the Smithsonian Institution Archives. "It was noted as missing and likely taken by an intern(实习生), from what the FBI is telling us. Word got out that it was missing when someone asked to see the letter for research purposes," and the intern put the letter back. "The intern likely took the letter again once nobody was watching it."

Decades passed. Finally, the FBI received a tip that the stolen document was located very close to Washington, D.C. Their art crime team recovered the letter but were unable to press charges because the time of limitations had ended. The FBI worked closely with the Archives to determine that the letter was both authentic and definitely Smithsonian's property.

The letter was written by Darwin to thank an American geologist, Dr. Ferdinand Vandeveer Hayden, for sending him copies of his research into the geology of the region that would become Yellowstone National Park.

The letter is in fairly good condition, in spite of being out of the care of trained museum staff for so long. "It was luckily in good shape," says Kapsalis, "and we just have to do some minor things in order to be able to unfold it. It has some glue on it that has colored it slightly, but nothing that will prevent us from using it. After it is repaired, we will take digital photos of it and that will be available online. One of our goals is to get items of high research value or interest to the public online."

It would now be difficult for an intern, visitor or a thief to steal a document like this. "Archiving practices have changed greatly since the 1970s," says Kapsalis, "and we keep our high value documents in a safe that I don't even have access to."

translation.source: 过去，乘飞机出行对大多数中国人来说是难以想象的。如今，随着经济的发展和生活水平的提高，越来越多的中国人包括许多农民和外出务工人员都能乘飞机出行。他们可以乘飞机到达所有大城市，还有很多城市也在筹建机场。航空服务不断改进，而且经常会有廉价机票。近年来，节假日期间选择乘飞机外出旅游的人数在不断增加。
translation.reference: In the past, it was unimaginable for most Chinese people to travel by air. Nowadays, with the development of the economy and the improvement of living standards, more and more Chinese people, including many farmers and migrant workers, can travel by air. They can reach all major cities by air, and many other cities are also planning to build airports. Meanwhile, air services are constantly improving, and discounted air tickets are often available. As a result, in recent years, the number of people who choose to travel by air during holidays has been increasing steadily.
